method_note: First pass (2026-11-14) used web-search snippets only. Verification pass (2026-11-14): pages on ciww.gov, kcci.com, iowapublicradio.org, nutrientstrategy.iastate.edu, ars.usda.gov, iowaagriculture.gov, extension.iastate.edu and waterservices.usgs.gov were fetched and read; 'primary' means the number was read on the fetched page and the quote is copied from it (PDF table rows are flattened text). nrcs.usda.gov and mymarketnews.ams.usda.gov dropped connections, and other hosts were blocked, so those facts stay 'secondary'. extra_quotes holds supporting quotes; inrs_2024_update holds the INRS Science Team's March 2024 revised efficiencies. Wording pass (2026-11-15): the CIWW cost page, the IPR 2025-06-20 ban story, the CIWW 193-day release, IPR 2026-06-09 and the INRS 2024 update PDF were re-fetched with curl and the quotes re-checked; www.epa.gov, littlevillagemag.com and bluewaterhealthyliving.com were blocked by the session proxy.

verification_levels.primary: number read by us on the fetched original page on 2026-11-14; quote copied from it
verification_levels.derived: our arithmetic from primary-verified inputs (e.g. day counts between verified dates)
verification_levels.secondary: number from search extraction, press, or a third party; original not opened
verification_levels.unverified: not confirmed; do not display as fact

facts.claim: Central Iowa Water Works' 12 member utilities serve more than 600,000 people in central Iowa.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works Returns to Everyday Water Stewardship as Nitrate Removal Facility Concludes 193-Days of Operation
facts.quote: Together, CIWW members serve more than 600,000 Iowans and distribute nearly 20 billion gallons of water each year.
facts.notes: Same 'more than 600,000' wording appears in the 2025 ban release and the 2026 Stage II releases. IPR (2026-06-09) calls it 'one in five Iowans'. Gallons conflict across CIWW releases ('nearly 22 billion' in 2025, 'nearly 20 billion' in 2026), so do not quote gallons. CIWW was chartered in April 2024; it is a regional authority of 12 founding members, not a merger.

facts.claim: The Fleur Drive nitrate removal facility can treat up to 10 million gallons a day with 8 ion-exchange vessels: at least 3 and up to 7 run at once, with one kept for regeneration.
facts.source_title: What is the Nitrate Removal Facility?
facts.quote: The facility includes eight treatment vessels and can process up to 10 million gallons of water per day. When operating, at least three vessels run at a time, and up to seven can operate simultaneously
facts.notes: Treated water is blended with other finished water. Scale: IPR 2025-06-25 quotes a DMWW chemist that 10 MGD is 'a fraction of normal demand, which can be 70-80 million gallons' (see fact nrf_vs_demand). Trigger: CIWW FAQ says the facility is used when source-water nitrate is elevated and lets CIWW meet the standard 'even when nitrate levels in the source water exceed 10 mg/L'. IPR 2026-01-12 says the facility can run as few as two vessels (CIWW FAQ says at least three); minor conflict, not important.

facts.claim: In 2025 the nitrate removal facility ran (partly or fully) on 112 days: 10-18 April and 28 April - 8 August 2025.
facts.source_title: Iowa water quality: Central Iowa Water Works officials lift irrigation restrictions
facts.quote: Central Iowa Water Works nitrate removal facility has operated for 112 days so far this year
facts.notes: Our check: 10-18 Apr = 9 days, 28 Apr - 8 Aug = 103 days, total 112. CIWW's own 29 Jul 2025 release (102 days through 29 Jul) agrees. KCCI (2026-03-04) repeats 'ran in part or fully for 112 days'. The quote is the in-article summary block (heading run into text). Facility ran 68 days in 2024 (secondary, not rechecked).

extra_quotes.quote: Central Iowa Water Works says its nitrate removal facility was shut down Friday, Aug. 8, after running at partial or full capacity since April 28 .
The plant was first turned on from April 10 to 18. In 2015, the facility ran for 177 days
The nitrate removal facility at the Fleur Drive plant continues to operate and has been in operation for 102 days through today.

facts.claim: Removing nitrate cost CIWW about $2.2 million in 2025: $1.6M operations & maintenance plus $0.6M capital.
facts.source_title: What is the Nitrate Removal Facility?
facts.quote: In 2025, the total annual cost was about $2.2 million, including $1.6 million in operations and maintenance and $600,000 in capital costs.
facts.notes: Say '$2.2M including capital' or '$1.6M to operate'; do not mix. Axios (2026-04-07, not opened) quotes Madsen: 'Last year, the cost was $1.6 million' = O&M only.

facts.claim: Operating and maintaining the nitrate removal facility cost about $1.6 million in 2025.
facts.source_title: What is the Nitrate Removal Facility?
facts.quote: In 2025, the total annual cost was about $2.2 million, including $1.6 million in operations and maintenance and $600,000 in capital costs.
facts.notes: Now sourced to the CIWW FAQ (read). Axios 2026-04-07 gives the same $1.6M (not opened; Axios host blocked).

facts.claim: At full capacity (7 vessels) the facility costs about $16,000 a day to run; partial operation costs less.
facts.source_title: What is the Nitrate Removal Facility?
facts.quote: When operating at full capacity (seven vessels), the Nitrate Removal Facility costs approximately $16,000 per day to run.
facts.notes: Upper bound, not average. Our arithmetic: 2025 O&M $1.6M / 112 operating days = about $14,300 per operating day. Axios 'about $11,000' and older '$10,000/day' figures were not rechecked; do not use. FLAG (2026-11-15): an earlier draft gave a $4,000/day low end (range lo); it is not on the CIWW page (re-fetched 2026-11-15) or any opened source, so the range was removed. Lower daily rates: 2025 O&M per run day (~$14k, our arithmetic) and Q1-2026 O&M per run day (~$8.4k, fact plant_cost_per_day_2026_q1_usd).

extra_quotes.quote: Operating the nitrate removal facility at Fleur Drive can cost $16,000 per day when operating at full capacity.

facts.claim: In the first quarter of 2026 the facility's O&M cost was about $660,000; CIWW says 2026 capital costs will be calculated in early 2027.
facts.source_title: What is the Nitrate Removal Facility?
facts.quote: In the first quarter of 2026, operations and maintenance costs were approximately $660,000. The 2026 capital costs will be calculated in early 2027.
facts.notes: CORRECTED wording: CIWW says the 2026 *capital* costs come in early 2027 (earlier draft said 'full 2026 costs'). No full-year 2026 O&M figure published as of 2026-11-14. Quote re-verified with curl on 2026-11-15. Per run day: see fact plant_cost_per_day_2026_q1_usd.

facts.claim: In Q1 2026 the nitrate removal facility's O&M cost averaged about $8,400 per run day: about $660,000 over 79 run days (6 Jan - 2 Mar and 9 - 31 Mar 2026).
facts.source_title: What is the Nitrate Removal Facility? (cost) + KCCI run dates
facts.quote: In the first quarter of 2026, operations and maintenance costs were approximately $660,000.
facts.notes: Our arithmetic: $660,000 / 79 = $8,354 per run day. Run days: 6 Jan - 2 Mar = 56, 9 - 31 Mar = 23 (KCCI 2026: 'It ran Jan. 6 through March 2. Operating resumed March 9'; see plant_days_2026 extra_quotes). Winter, partial operation: use as a lower daily rate (e.g. 2026 estimate 193 days x $8.4k-16k = $1.6-3.1M). Cost quote re-fetched with curl 2026-11-15.

facts.claim: In 2026 the nitrate removal facility ran a record 193 days: 6 Jan - 2 Mar and 9 Mar - 23 Jul 2026. The previous record was 177 days in 2015.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works returns to everyday water stewardship as Nitrate Removal Facility concludes 193 days of operation
facts.quote: The decision follows the conclusion of operations at the Nitrate Removal Facility, which ran for 193 days during the 2026 season before being taken offline on Thursday, July 23, 2026.
facts.notes: Our check: 6 Jan - 2 Mar = 56 days, 9 Mar - 23 Jul = 137 days, total 193. So it was NOT continuous: KCCI (2026-07-28) says '193 straight days', which conflicts with KCCI's own March reports of a one-week stop. Say '193 days', not '193 straight days'. WeAreIowa's 192 is an outlier. No fall-2026 restart found as of 2026-11-14. 'Record' (2026-11-15 check): the CIWW 193-day release (re-fetched) does not use the word 'record'. 'Longest run on record' is our comparison with fact plant_days_record_prior (177 days in 2015: KCCI 2025-08-12 and IPR 2026-06-09, 'The record was set in 2015 with 177 days', re-fetched). Search snippets show the Des Moines Register and Little Village calling 193 days 'record-setting', but those pages were blocked and not opened. App label: '193 days (Jan-Jul)', longest on record (previous most: 177 days in 2015).

extra_quotes.quote: It ran Jan. 6 through March 2. Operating resumed March 9 and continues through today.
As of Monday, Kahler said the Fleur Drive nitrate removal facility had run for 148 days in 2026, representing about 95% of the year so far.

facts.claim: Before 2026, the longest nitrate removal run was 177 days, in 2015.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works nitrate removal facility turns off, running for 112 days so far this year
facts.quote: In 2015, the facility ran for 177 days
facts.notes: Two outlets read directly agree.

extra_quotes.quote: The record was set in 2015 with 177 days.

facts.claim: CIWW's first-ever lawn-watering ban (Stage III) began 12 June 2025 because nitrate in the Raccoon and Des Moines rivers was near record levels and nitrate removal was already at full capacity.
facts.source_title: CIWW Resumes Commercial Irrigation, Continuing The Phased Exit From The Stage III Watering Ban
facts.quote: commercial irrigation and lawn watering can resume on Wednesday, July 30, as part of the phased exit from the Stage III lawn watering ban initiated on June 12.
facts.notes: The ban release itself (ciww.gov/?p=48) shows no date on the page; its WordPress post date (2025-06-06) is a site-migration artifact. Date confirmed by CIWW 29 Jul 2025 release, IPR and KCCI. Run-up: voluntary 25% cut from 30 May 2025, 50% request 11 Jun (KCCI 2025-08-15). 'First-ever': IPR 2025-06-20 (quote in extra_quotes, fetched 2026-11-15); see fact ban_2025_first_ever.

extra_quotes.quote: Central Iowa Water Works needs to limit the amount of river water that is used in the treatment process because nitrate concentrations in the Raccoon and Des Moines rivers have climbed to near record levels.
Central Iowa Water Works has been removing nitrate using the nitrate removal facility for more than 55 days. All nitrate removal processes are operating at full capacity
Central Iowa Water Works issued a lawn watering ban June 12
The Des Moines area’s first-ever lawn watering ban has been in effect for over a week .

facts.claim: The June 2025 Stage III ban was the Des Moines area's first-ever lawn-watering ban; compliance cut demand by more than 30%, letting CIWW keep pace with nitrate removal and meet federal standards.
facts.source_title: Des Moines lawn watering ban (Iowa Public Radio, 2025-06-20)
facts.quote: The Des Moines area’s first-ever lawn watering ban has been in effect for over a week . Central Iowa Water Works (CIWW) said compliance reduced demand by over 30%, allowing the regional utility to keep pace with nitrate removal and meet federal standards.
facts.notes: Fetched with curl 2026-11-15; quote copied from the page text (the stray space before the full stop is a link boundary on the page). The 'meet federal standards' part is CIWW's statement as reported by IPR for June 2025 only; the app does not claim the tap met the standard.

facts.claim: The 2025 ban was first eased for residential customers on 22 July 2025.
facts.source_title: Lawn Watering To Resume July 22 Following A Phased Approach!
facts.quote: On July 18, 2025, the Technical Committee voted to lift the ban on residential lawn watering beginning Tuesday, July 22 .
facts.notes: Phase 1 residential 22 Jul; phase 2 commercial 30 Jul (CIWW 29 Jul release); phase 3 local governments and schools 7 Aug (KCCI). Trigger used: nitrate in at least one source (the infiltration gallery) at or below 10 mg/L for a sustained period (CIWW 18 Jul 2025 release).

facts.claim: CIWW ended the Stage III lawn-watering ban on 7 Aug 2025 (moved to Stage I, voluntary 25% cut); all restrictions ended 15 Aug 2025.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works ends lawn watering ban, moves to voluntary reduction stage
facts.quote: Central Iowa Water Works has ended the Stage III lawn watering ban, it announced Thursday.
facts.notes: KCCI article datePublished 2025-08-07 (a Thursday). The CIWW site has no 7 Aug 2025 release in its news feed. IWLA's 'June 12 to July 31, 49 days' is WRONG.

extra_quotes.quote: Residents under Central Iowa Water Works are now under the Stage I plan, which calls for a voluntary reduction of outside watering by 25%. Local governments and school districts can now resume lawn watering efforts.
Officials loosened the restrictions in July and now, effective Friday, Aug. 15, it's been fully lifted.

facts.claim: The mandatory 2025 Stage III lawn-watering ban lasted 56 days for all customers (12 Jun - 7 Aug 2025); homes were under the full ban for 40 days (to 22 Jul) and businesses for 48 days (to 30 Jul).
facts.source_title: Derived from CIWW ban start/end releases
facts.notes: Our arithmetic from primary-verified dates: 12 Jun -> 22 Jul = 40 d (residential), -> 30 Jul = 48 d (commercial), -> 7 Aug = 56 d (governments/schools, end of Stage III). Any restriction (Stage I-III) 30 May - 15 Aug = 77 days.

facts.claim: CIWW imposed its second mandatory lawn-watering ban on 8 June 2026, covering about 600,000 people.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works Issues Stage 3 “Water Warning” Lawn Watering Ban Effective Immediately
facts.quote: West Des Moines, Iowa (June 8, 2026) – The Central Iowa Water Works (CIWW) Board of Trustees has initiated Stage 3 of its Water Use Plan,implementing a mandatory lawn watering ban for residential, business, and government customers across the region.
facts.notes: Preceded by Stage II voluntary request on 27 May 2026 (CIWW release). IPR 2026-06-09: Stage III considered when demand exceeds 90% of treatment capacity (fact stage3_trigger_demand_pct). Quote copied verbatim incl. the missing space in 'Plan,implementing'.

facts.claim: Residential customers were moved off the 2026 lawn-watering ban (to Stage II, 50% voluntary cut) on 1 July 2026; the ban stayed for business and government customers until 20 July.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works Eases Restrictions Through Phased Approach to Stage II
facts.quote: The change is effective immediately for residential customers. The lawn watering ban will remain in effect for commercial and governmental customers
facts.notes: Release dateline: WEST DES MOINES, Iowa (July 1, 2026). CIWW 9 Jul 2026 release confirms the business/government ban continued.

facts.claim: Residential customers left the 2026 lawn-watering ban on 1 July 2026; business and government customers on 20 July 2026. All restrictions ended 27 July 2026.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works Transitions All Customers to Stage II Water Use Restrictions
facts.quote: Effective July 20, 2026, residential, commercial, and governmental customers may resume outdoor irrigation while reducing lawn watering by approximately 50% and following the regional even/odd lawn watering schedule.
facts.notes: CONFLICT RESOLVED: CIWW's 1 Jul 2026 release moved residential customers to Stage II that day; 20 Jul moved the remaining (business/government) customers. 27 Jul = all restrictions ended (CIWW 193-day release dated 27 Jul).

extra_quotes.quote: The change is effective immediately for residential customers. The lawn watering ban will remain in effect for commercial and governmental customers
The Central Iowa Water Works (CIWW) Technical Committee met today and voted to return to everyday water stewardship, ending all mandatory and voluntary water use restrictions.

facts.claim: The 2026 mandatory lawn-watering ban lasted 23 days for homes (8 Jun - 1 Jul) and 42 days for business and government customers (8 Jun - 20 Jul 2026).
facts.source_title: Derived from CIWW 2026 releases
facts.notes: Our arithmetic from primary-verified dates; CIWW itself says '23 days' on 1 Jul. Any restriction (Stage II voluntary from 27 May to 27 Jul) = 61 days; Stage III to all-clear (8 Jun - 27 Jul) = 49 days. Compare 2025: 40 days for homes, 56 days to end of Stage III.

extra_quotes.quote: Significant conservation efforts of residents and businesses in the region over the past 23 days have reduced water use

facts.claim: To fully lift the 2025 ban, CIWW said at least one source must read 10 mg/L nitrate or less; it later kept the ban until both rivers showed a steady downward trend.
facts.source_title: Stage III Daily Updates
facts.quote: One of many factors to fully lift the ban requires that at least one water source – either the Raccoon River or Des Moines River – record nitrate concentrations at 10 mg/L or less.
facts.notes: In practice the 2025 release was triggered by the infiltration gallery (not a river) staying below 10 mg/L. No explicit 2026 lift criterion published; 2026 releases cite falling demand and improving source-water conditions.

extra_quotes.quote: we needed to see nitrate concentrations in at least one water source decline to 10 mg/l and stay there for a sustained period. This week, that happened in the Infiltration Gallery.

facts.claim: In 2025 the Raccoon River peaked at 20.55 mg/L nitrate-N on 8 June (only the second time above 20).
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works shows how its Des Moines plant tests and treats drinking water with nitrates
facts.quote: On June 8, the Raccoon River hit 20.55 mg/L. A Central Iowa Water Works spokesperson said it marked the second time nitrate in the river surpassed 20 mg/L.
facts.notes: CIWW lab value as reported by IPR. CONFLICT (not re-opened): IPR 2025-08-06 says 19.39 mg/L on 9 Jun. USGS sensor (05484500, param 99133) daily-mean maximum in 2025 = 18.4 mg/L on 7 Jun (our query of waterservices dv). Sensor daily means sit below lab grab peaks; label which one is shown.

facts.claim: In 2025 the Des Moines River peaked at about 17 mg/L nitrate-N on 12 June.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works shows how its Des Moines plant tests and treats drinking water with nitrates
facts.quote: On June 12, nitrate in the Des Moines River reached 17.15 mg/L — below the record 18.62 mg/L in 2013.
facts.notes: CONFLICT: IPR 2025-08-06 says 16.66; Iowa Capital Dispatch 16.6 (neither re-opened). USGS 05482000 daily-mean maximum 2025 = 17.0 mg/L on 12 Jun (our waterservices query).

facts.claim: The record Raccoon River nitrate level is 24.39 mg/L, set in 2013.
facts.source_title: Central Iowa Water Works shows how its Des Moines plant tests and treats drinking water with nitrates
facts.quote: The record was set in 2013 with 24.39 mg/L.
facts.notes: Des Moines River record 18.62 mg/L (2013), same article. 2025 was 'near record', NOT a record.

facts.claim: In 2026 the USGS sensor on the Raccoon River at Van Meter recorded a maximum daily mean of 18.6 mg/L nitrate-N (28 May 2026); higher than the earlier-cited 17.45 mg/L (25 Jan).
facts.source_title: USGS NWIS daily values, 05484500, parameter 99133
facts.notes: CORRECTED: 17.45 (25 Jan, search-only attribution to CIWW TC minutes) is not the 2026 high; the Jan 14 TC minutes we opened do not contain 17.45. Our USGS query: 2026 daily means include provisional ('P') data and ~67 missing days through 13 Nov. For comparison 2025 max daily mean 18.4 (7 Jun). 2026 was a record for DURATION, not peak concentration.

facts.claim: By 8 June 2026 the Raccoon River had been above 10 mg/L for 136 days that year, and the Des Moines River for 117 days.
facts.source_title: Why has CIWW implemented a lawn watering ban?
facts.quote: As of June 8, 2026, the Raccoon River has measured nitrate concentrations above 10 mg/L for 136 days, the Des Moines River has registered 117 days over 10mg/L
facts.notes: Same page: NRF operating about 95% of the year; about 50% of Maffitt Reservoir storage already used. Our USGS daily-mean count for the full 2026 to 13 Nov: Raccoon 176 days > 10 mg/L (with data gaps).

facts.claim: Iowa lawmakers appropriated $25 million (2026) to expand CIWW's nitrate removal facility.
facts.source_title: KCCI Investigates: $1.2 billion in Central Iowa Water Works projects coming
facts.quote: For instance, expanding the nitrate removal facility got a $25 million appropriation from state lawmakers.
facts.notes: 'Double capacity within three years' comes from a KDSM headline/search snippet only (kdsm17.com blocked); not read. Part of the 2026 'Farm to Faucet' water quality package (IDALS 2026-06-22 page names the package).

facts.claim: Doubling the nitrate removal facility is estimated to cost about $40 million; ratepayers would cover what the $25M state grant does not.
facts.source_title: KCCI Investigates: $1.2 billion in Central Iowa Water Works projects coming
facts.quote: The estimated cost right now is $40 million. Ratepayers would make up the difference.
facts.notes: KCCI 2026-07-28 said 'more than $25 million'; an earlier KCCI estimate was $23M construction (search only). The ~$1.2B CIWW capital program is mostly growth-driven (KCCI: 'as we grow, we need more water'); do not call it a nitrate cost.

facts.claim: A Polk County-commissioned, 2-year study by 16 scientists (CISWRA, July 2025) attributed roughly 70-80% of nitrate in the Raccoon and Des Moines rivers to agriculture (about 40% surplus fertilizer).
facts.source_title: Polk County research report confirms nitrate in rivers directly tied to agriculture
facts.publisher: Yahoo News / Iowa PBS Market to Market
facts.notes: Report itself not opened. KCCI (read) states 80%; Iowa PBS summary (search) >70%, with 40% surplus fertilizer, 20% manure, 20% soybean-fixed; Axios 2026-08-18: manure 12-19%, cities 1.5-2%. Prefer the INRS statewide nonpoint figure (fact inrs_nonpoint_share_pct, primary) on slides, or say 'roughly 70-80% from agriculture'.

extra_quotes.quote: A report commissioned by Polk County leaders had 16 scientists conclude that 80% of the nitrate pollution comes from agricultural land.

facts.claim: In an average year, an Iowa acre of corn or soybeans loses about 30 lb of nitrogen as nitrate to waterways.
facts.source_title: The Science Behind Nitrate Transport
facts.notes: Range: ISU Gilmore City drainage site averaged ~36 lb N/ac at 150-160 lb N fertilizer, varying 0.9-94 lb/ac by weather; ~15-20 lb/ac even with no N. ISU Extension: normal 15-25, wet springs 40-50 lb/ac. Corn and soybean losses are similar. STILL SECONDARY: stories.cals.iastate.edu and crops.extension.iastate.edu are blocked for this session; not on an allowed host.

facts.claim: In a 14-year USDA-ARS tile-drainage experiment near Ames, a cereal rye cover crop cut nitrate load by 57% (concentration by 59%).
facts.source_title: Impact of broadcasting a cereal rye or oat cover crop before corn and soybean harvest on nitrate (Kaspar, Jaynes, Parkin, Moorman 2016, ASA-CSSA-SSSA abstract)
facts.quote: Over 14 years a cereal rye cover crop reduced nitrate concentrations by 59% and nitrate load by 57%.
facts.notes: USDA-ARS long-term tile-drainage experiment near Ames (no-till rye). It is a meeting abstract summarising the long-term site. Kaspar et al. 2007 JEQ (4 yr): 61% load; 2012 AWM: rye 48%, oat 26% (concentration) - not re-opened.

facts.claim: At other Iowa sites, Kaspar reports rye cover crops cut nitrate 15-48% (on-farm 2016: 40% lower load). Effects depend on rye growth, soil, weather and drainage timing.
facts.source_title: Winter Cover Crop Impacts on Erosion and Nitrate Losses in Tile Drainage (Kaspar SARE presentation)
facts.notes: The concept doc's '22-48%' was NOT found; the source found gives 15-48%. Use 15-48%. sare.org blocked; not rechecked.

facts.claim: Iowa's Nutrient Reduction Strategy science assessment estimates a cereal rye cover crop cuts nitrate-N concentration in drainage by 31% on average (SD 29).
facts.source_title: Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy (Feb 2025), Section 2: Iowa Science Assessment of Nonpoint Source Practices, Table 2
facts.notes: 2025 INRS Section 2 (Feb 2025), Table 2, PDF p. 6. Values are % reduction in nitrate-N concentration, mean (SD), from a literature review; the Feb 2025 edition still prints the original 2013 values. Corn yield change -6% (SD 7) in the 2025 table. The Science Team's 2024 literature update (Mar 2024) revises rye to 28 (26) rotational average (corn year 27, soybean year 30) and its corn-yield effect to 0 (10). Show 31% as the official INRS table value, or 28% as the 2024 update - label which.

Values are % reduction in nitrate-N concentration, mean (SD), from a literature review; the Feb 2025 edition still prints the original 2013 values. Column header 'Average (SD*)' and footnote '* SD = standard deviation' confirmed on the page. 2024 update SD = 26.
